title: Watts and the Too-Perfect Street
description: An ordinary-looking dog with an extraordinary bright secret discovers something strange on Marigold Lane.

passages.text: On Marigold Lane, every house had a pink front door. Every hedge was a perfect square. Every garden gnome pointed exactly north. At six o’clock, every neighbor stepped outside, waved three times, and said, “What a lovely, lovely evening.”

Watts lived at number twelve. He was a small golden-brown dog with floppy ears, a white patch on his chest, and a red collar. He liked running. He liked sniffing. He especially liked things that weren’t where they belonged.

A crooked daisy! A dropped mitten! A sandwich crust beneath a bench! Marigold Lane didn’t approve of dropped things. Watts approved of them very much. He gave the daisy a sniff, the mitten a sniff, and the sandwich crust a very careful investigation.

Then the sun slipped behind the rooftops. A little boy on the nearest porch dropped his toy bus into the dark space beneath the steps. “Oh,” he whispered. “I can’t see it.” Watts pricked his ears. He knew something useful about darkness.

Pop! Where the dog had stood, a light bulb floated in the air. Its glass shone honey-gold. Watts had no paws now, and no wagging tail. But he could light up the steps, the flowerpots, and the little blue bus.

“There it is!” said the boy. He reached beneath the steps and pulled it out. “Thank you, light.” Watts glowed a little brighter. Saying thank you to a light bulb was an excellent idea, although most people forgot to do it.

When the bus was safely rescued, Watts thought of running. Pop! Four paws touched the path. He shook his ears and trotted toward home. Being a bulb was useful. Being a dog was better for investigating sandwich crusts.

But before he reached the gate, every porch light went out. Not one after another. All together. The lane fell silent. Even the sprinklers stopped their tick-tick-ticking. From behind a hedge came a soft sound: shuff, shuff, shuff.

A tall man in a plum-colored coat was creeping between the houses. His pointed hat brushed the hedge. Wherever his gray glove passed, something strange happened. A garden gnome lifted one stone foot. Then it lifted the other.

The gnome walked backward across the lawn. A perfectly square hedge shivered without any wind. A mailbox opened its little mouth and whispered, “Hooooome.” Watts planted all four paws on the pavement. This man was making trouble on purpose.

His name was Mr. Hush. He liked dark windows and empty streets. He liked making people hide behind their curtains. When a frightened face disappeared from a window, he tipped his hat and gave a nasty little chuckle.

Watts growled. Mr. Hush looked down. “Go home, little dog.” Watts barked instead. A good, loud, ordinary bark. Somewhere a curtain moved. “None of that,” snapped Mr. Hush. He swept his glove toward the next house and hurried away.

Watts ran after him. Past the first pink door. Past the second pink door. Past the third pink door, which was so much like the others that Watts nearly chased his own reflection in its shiny brass letterbox.

Mr. Hush flicked his fingers. Long shadows slid out beneath the hedges. They curled across the pavement like enormous black shoelaces. Watts jumped one, ducked beneath another, and landed beside a dustbin with a terrific CLONK.
The lid rolled down the path. Mr. Hush jumped at the noise. His hat tilted over one eye. For a moment, he didn’t look very powerful. He looked like a man who badly needed to find his hat.

Watts noticed something else. Whenever Mr. Hush passed beneath the last glow of a window, he hurried into deeper shade. He hugged the hedges. He avoided the bright kitchen. Perhaps, thought Watts, this was a job for his other shape.

Pop! Watts became a light bulb. Golden light spread across the path. The nearest shadow shrank to a little puddle beneath a rosebush. The walking gnome stopped with one foot in the air. Mr. Hush squeaked and darted behind a thick hedge.

Watts shone at the hedge. Every leaf turned bright green. A sleepy caterpillar blinked. But the man was on the other side, where the light couldn’t reach. “You missed,” Mr. Hush whispered. “A hedge is a very useful thing.”

Watts drifted left. Mr. Hush shuffled right. Watts drifted right. Mr. Hush shuffled left. Round and round they went, until the caterpillar tucked its head away as if to say, Some of us are trying to sleep.

Watts stopped. Chasing a man around a hedge could take all night. He needed somewhere open. Somewhere without a wall or a bush to hide behind. Then he remembered the grassy little hill at the end of Marigold Lane.
Pop! Watts was a dog again. He bounded out from the hedge, scooped Mr. Hush’s long trailing coat hem in his mouth, and gave one quick tug. Then he let go and ran toward the hill.

“Come back!” cried Mr. Hush. Watts paused, looked over his shoulder, and wagged his ordinary dog tail. Mr. Hush stamped after him. Watts ran a little farther. Mr. Hush followed. Up the grassy slope they went.

At the top, Watts stopped beneath the wide night sky. No tall hedge. No garden wall. No porch to duck behind. Just grass, stars, a crooked hat, and one very cross bad guy. Below them, the neighbors peeked out of their windows.

“Now,” said Mr. Hush, reaching out one gray glove, “I’ve got you.” Watts didn’t bark. He didn’t growl. He simply looked at the man, thought of the little blue bus, and remembered how good it felt to help someone see.

Pop! Watts became a light bulb. He shone straight at Mr. Hush. There was nowhere for the bad guy to hide. Golden light touched his shoes, his gloves, his long plum coat, and the very tip of his pointed hat.

And Mr. Hush disappeared. Not down the hill. Not behind a tree. He vanished altogether, like a bad dream when someone opens the curtains. One moment he was there. The next there was nothing but clear, bright air.

All along Marigold Lane, the strange shadows slipped back beneath the things they belonged to. The mailbox stopped whispering. The gnome set down its foot. The porch lights blinked on, one by one, until the street twinkled below the hill.

Watts stayed bright for a little while. He lit the path so the neighbors could step outside together. Their waves weren’t matching now. Some people waved twice. Some waved with both hands. One lady forgot to wave because she was hugging her husband.

Pop! Watts became a dog and ran down to meet them. The little boy brought his blue bus. His grandmother brought a bowl of water. Someone found a biscuit. Watts thought this was a very sensible way to celebrate.

The neighbors stayed outside talking. One hedge had a crooked corner. One gnome faced sideways. Nobody hurried to straighten them. “What a lovely evening,” said the grandmother. This time, everyone said it at a different moment.

At last Watts curled up on his cushion at number twelve. His ears drooped. His paws twitched with one final, sleepy run. Across the lane, the boy put his bus beside his bed and whispered, “Good night, Watts.”

The houses grew quiet. The crooked daisy nodded in the breeze. Watts closed his eyes beneath the warm porch lamp. Tomorrow there would be paths to run, things to sniff, and perhaps someone who needed a little light.

scenes.alt: Watts the ordinary golden-brown dog explores a perfectly tidy suburban street.
Watts becomes a glowing light bulb above the porch steps, helping a child find a toy bus.
Watts discovers Mr. Hush making a garden gnome walk through an eerie suburban garden.
Watts chases Mr. Hush while strange long shadows stretch across the lane.
Watts shines as a light bulb but the villain hides behind a thick garden hedge.
Watts lures Mr. Hush onto an open grassy hill beneath the stars.
Watts shines brightly on the hill and Mr. Hush disappears in the golden light.
Watts is an ordinary dog again, resting on his porch as his safe neighborhood settles for the night.
